title: Why trailers are called trailers
hook: Trailers got their name because they once came after the main feature, not before.
peek: Trailers now arrive before the main feature, but the name points to an older habit. In early cinemas, adverts for coming films were often shown after the feature, trailing it. Historians argue over how common this was, but the name stuck.
lede: It seems odd to call something that plays first a trailer. The usual explanation is that early American cinemas often ran previews of coming attractions at the end of the programme, trailing the main film. As audiences tended to leave as soon as the feature ended, cinemas moved them to the start. Historians note the evidence is patchy, but the name stayed put.

bullets.text: One of the earliest known trailers was put together in 1913 by Nils Granlund, an advertising manager for the Loew's theatre chain in New York. He filmed rehearsals of a stage musical, The Pleasure Seekers, and showed them in cinemas.

Cliffhanger film serials of the 1910s often ended with a short tease for the next episode, shown after the chapter had finished. These end-of-show promotions are one strong root of the word and the habit.

From 1919, a company called National Screen Service made most American trailers for decades, with stock title cards, narrators and big lettering. Studios took the work in house in later years and trailers became a craft of their own.

In 2014, American cinema owners asked studios to keep trailers to two minutes, down from the older two minutes thirty, with two longer exceptions a year. The guideline is voluntary, and many trailers still run longer.
